Getting Started with R

Part 8: Creating an R Project

At this point, we’re starting to move away from the more theoretical content about how R works, and toward some practical applications for doing data analysis. This tutorial will demonstrate how to create an R project.


  • To create an R project, click on the File menu and choose “New Project”.

  • You can either create a new folder for your project, or put it in an existing folder. To create a new folder, choose “New Directory” and then “New Project”.

  • In the New Project Wizard that comes up, you can name your project and choose where you want it to go on your computer.
  • I’m going to call this one “Demo Project”, and create it as a subdirectory of the “R Tutorials” folder.

  • When you click “Create Project”, it takes a moment to load, but when it does, R has switched to a new, blank session.
    • All the tabs that were open in your previous session are no longer present.
    • The Files window shows the inside of your project folder, which now has one file in it, an .Rproj file with the same name as the folder.

  • And if we set our working directory, it has been set to this “Demo Project” folder.
getwd()
## [1] "C:/Users/ksb89187/OneDrive - University of Georgia/Documents/R Tutorials/Demo Project"
  • From here, you can build out a file structure to store the files you’ll be using and creating in your project.
  • In the output pane, go to “New Folder”, and you can create whatever file structure is useful to you.

  • It’s good practice to at least have a folder for your data, a folder for your scripts, and a folder for your results (things you create in R, like graphs or statistical models).

  • To exit a project and go back to your regular RStudio screen, with all the tabs you previously had open, go to the File menu and choose “Close Project”.

  • Now when we check our working directory, it has returned to being the home base “Documents” folder.
getwd()
## [1] "C:/Users/ksb89187/OneDrive - University of Georgia/Documents"
  • You can reopen a project by:
    • In R, going to “File” > “Open Project”, navigating into your project folder, and double-clicking the .Rproj file
    • Double-clicking the .Rproj file from the regular file explorer.

  • Sometimes, you may want to create the file structure of a project before you create the R project itself.
  • Here, I have a folder called “Existing Project”, and I’ve already built it out to include:
    • a data folder, a documentation folder, a results folder, and a scripts folder
    • sample data in the data folder

  • To add an R project to this folder, we can go to RStudio, go to “New Project”, and choose “Existing Directory”.

  • From there, we can browse to the correct folder, and create our project in the root directory.
  • It should be on the same level as all of the folders, not inside any of them.

  • Choose “Open” and “Create Project”, and then the output pane will show that we are now in the “Existing Project” folder and an “Existing Project.Rproj” file has been added to the folder.

  • One thing to note is that creating a project isn’t mandatory to work with R. You always have the option to pull up RStudio and immediately start typing your code into a script, or open a saved R file from anywhere on your computer.
  • However, working from within an R project can make it easier to keep track of your files.
    • An R project will keep all your scripts, datasets, and outputs in the same place, and will set your working directory to be very local, so you won’t have to type out the full filepath for every file you want to access.
    • Also, if you change where you R project is located on your computer, all the internal filepaths will remain the same, because their structure inside the folder is still the same, and the only thing that has changed is the path TO the working directory.
  • So projects can be a very useful tool in your data analysis workflow.
